## Preliminaries

**Working scope (declared as assumption, not fact).** Jonah 1:1-17 is taken as a single reading unit for this debate. Unlike Dan 1 or Dan 3 (split across two debates each, for a clear internal division — a decree followed by a separately-narrated later outcome, or a scene-change across a time-gap), Jonah 1 runs as one uninterrupted causal chain, verse to verse: the call (1:1-2) produces the flight (1:3), which is followed immediately by the storm (1:4), which produces the sailors' fear and Jonah's contrasting sleep (1:5), the captain's rebuke (1:6), the lot (1:7), the interrogation (1:8), Jonah's confession (1:9), the sailors' escalated fear (1:10), their question and the worsening sea (1:11), Jonah's self-offering (1:12), their attempted alternative (1:13), their prayer (1:14), the casting-out and calm (1:15), their worship (1:16), and the LORD's appointment of the fish (1:17) — no time-skip or scene-relocation breaks this sequence internally. This is the same "textually one unit" judgment applied to Dan 4:1-37 at similar length. The working assumption is that "bearing on the inner being" here includes: (a) Jonah's own stated and unstated interior throughout, since he is the addressed and analysed human across the whole chapter, even though his own stated interior surfaces only twice (1:9, 1:12); (b) the sailors — the mariners, the captain, and "the men" collectively — treated per step 2 notes (b)-(f) as a collective and, where the text individuates them ("each... his god," the captain alone), as individuated candidates, not dismissed as scenery; (c) the LORD's own actions, in scope per note (b) as a non-human being whose acts are stated in direct, repeated relation to the humans in the passage; (d) the storm, sea, ship, and fish, in scope per note (b)/(d) as non-human elements whose states are inseparable from, and directly bear on, the humans' own crisis and response throughout.

**Reading rule applied.** No [AMBIGUOUS]-span STEP-live resolution was needed — the base extract reports 100% meaning coverage for this range (220/220 non-particle spans). Hebrew narrative prose throughout (contrast the Aramaic court-tale genre of Daniel 2-7); glosses and roots are read as given in the base extract, no external lexical input added (Part B.7).

**Corpus-continuity check.** No prior filled debate found for this book at or before this range — this is the first debate in the sequence (or nothing precedes it yet). Nothing to re-read.

## Per-verse debate

### Jon 1:1

> Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,

**Observation.** "The word [H1697G] of the LORD [H3068G] came [H1961] to [H0413] Jonah [H3124] the son [H1121A] of Amittai [H0573], saying [H0559/H9005]."

**Operation 1 — the LORD's word coming to Jonah.**
- **Action-type:** came/was-given (a word-event).
- **Subject:** the LORD (non-human, in scope per note (b) — its action is directed at Jonah, the human in focus).
- **Operation:** a movement — the word "coming to" Jonah (H1961 "to be/happen" + H0413 "to/toward").
- **Source:** self — the LORD's own initiative, explicit ("the word of the LORD").
- **Target:** Jonah.

**Interrogative — questions considered.** (`WA-interpretation-questions` Q1-Q11 — every human mentioned in this verse is a presumptive candidate, per read-guidance step 2 note (f); a candidate that resolves to nothing is recorded as an explicit silence, per Part B.4, not omitted)
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — focused inner being; but this verse states nothing of his reception or interior, only that the word "came to" him — the book's first candidate silence, and notable given that this is a book about a prophet whose response is about to be narrated by act (1:3), not by stated feeling.
- Q3: The coming-of-the-word is itself stated as an event. Jonah's own interior at receiving it is unstated.
- Q4: Source of the word = the LORD, self, explicit. Jonah's own response has no stated source in this verse.
- Q5: Target = Jonah.
- Q6: A movement — the word "came to" him.
- Q7: Direct forward linkage to 1:2 (the word's content) and 1:3 (Jonah's response, given by act, not stated interior).
- Q8: N/A — Jonah is individuated.
- Q9: Sufficient for what is stated.
- Q11: came/was-given.

**Decision.** Retain as a stated IB operation (divine initiative). Jonah's own reception is recorded as an explicit, named silence (Part B.4) — carried forward to see whether later verses resolve it (they do not resolve it directly; see 1:3).

### Jon 1:2

> “ Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.”

**Observation.** "Arise [H6965B], go [H1980G] to Nineveh [H5210], that great [H1419A] city [H5892B], and call out [H7121I] against [H5921A] it, for their evil [H7451I] has come up [H5927G] before [H6440G] me [H9020]."

**Operation 1 — the LORD's command to Jonah.**
- **Action-type:** commanded/commissioned.
- **Subject:** the LORD.
- **Operation:** a movement — a directive issued to Jonah, sending him toward Nineveh.
- **Source:** self — the LORD's own initiative.
- **Target:** Jonah (recipient of the command); Nineveh (object of the commanded act).

**Operation 2 — Nineveh's evil, "come up" before the LORD (the mission's stated cause).**
- **Action-type:** sinned/ascended (a condition reported reaching God).
- **Subject:** Nineveh — a human collective ("that great city," standing for its inhabitants, per step 2 note (c)).
- **Operation:** a movement — "their evil has come up" (H5927, ascend) — an emergent condition rising to reach the LORD's awareness.
- **Source:** Nineveh itself — the collective's own doing ("their evil"), not attributed externally.
- **Target:** the LORD ("before me").

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — the command's addressee; his own interior at receiving it is not stated here either, continuing the silence from 1:1. Nineveh — a human collective (note (c)); its "evil" is a stated collective condition, though nothing is yet said of any individual disposition or awareness within it.
- Q3: Nineveh's evil is stated, explicitly, as divine testimony ("their evil has come up before me") — not inferred. Jonah's reception remains unstated.
- Q4: Source of the command = the LORD, self. Source of Nineveh's evil = the collective itself, self-caused.
- Q5: Target of the command = Jonah; target of Nineveh's evil (its effect) = the LORD.
- Q6: Both movements — a command going out, and evil "coming up."
- Q7: Direct linkage to 1:1 (the word now given content) and forward to 1:3 (Jonah's response — flight, not compliance); a further forward linkage to the book's later chapters (Nineveh's actual repentance, Jonah 3), outside this passage but worth naming as an open thread.
- Q8: Nineveh as collective ("that great city") reshapes the operation as directed at a whole population, not an individual, per note (c).
- Q9: Sufficient for what is stated.
- Q11: commanded/commissioned (LORD→Jonah); sinned/ascended (Nineveh's evil).

**Decision.** Retain both operations. Jonah's continued silence (his reception of the command) is carried forward — first tested by his response in 1:3, which is behavioral (flight), not a stated interior reason.

### Jon 1:3

> But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord.

**Observation.** "Jonah [H3124] rose [H6965B] to flee [H1272/H9005] to Tarshish [H8659H] from the presence [H6440H] of the LORD [H3068G]. He went down [H3381], found [H4672] a ship [H0591] going [H0935G] to Tarshish, paid [H5414N] the fare [H7939], and went down [H3381/H9024] into it, to go [H0935G] with them [H9038] to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD."

**Operation 1 — Jonah's rising to flee (the decision-act).**
- **Action-type:** fled (rose-to-flee).
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a movement — going away from the LORD's presence.
- **Source:** self — his own act; no external causer stated.
- **Target:** "away from the presence of the LORD" (a relational target — distancing from the LORD).

**Operation 2 — Jonah's flight sequence executed (down to Joppa, ship found, fare paid, boarded).**
- **Action-type:** fled (continued/executed).
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a movement — a chain of go-down/find/pay/go-down-into acts in service of the same flight.
- **Source:** self.
- **Target:** Tarshish (the intended destination); "away from the presence of the LORD," restated at the verse's close — the phrase brackets the whole verse.

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: Jonah is the focused inner being throughout, but the flight is reported entirely as a stated ACT; per step 3 note (e), whatever disposition drove it (fear, defiance, reluctance) may be "hidden behind" the act, with only the act recorded. The text never states Jonah's motive within this passage (it is stated only later, at Jonah 4:2, outside this passage's scope).
- Q3: The act is stated (rose, fled, went down, found, paid, went down). The interior/motive behind it is NOT stated anywhere in this chapter — an explicit, named silence (Part B.4), with a forward-pointer to Jonah 4:2.
- Q4: Source of the flight-act = self. Source of the disposition behind it = unstated within this passage.
- Q5: Target = "away from the presence of the LORD" (stated twice, bracketing the verse) and Tarshish.
- Q6: Movement, repeatedly.
- Q7: Direct linkage back to 1:2 (the command just given) — the flight's direction (away from Nineveh, toward Tarshish) invites a refusal-reading, but the text itself never uses a word for "refuse" or "disobey" here; that reading is an inference from the geography, flagged as interpretive (Part B.3), not asserted as bald textual fact. Forward linkage to 1:4 (the LORD's response) and to Jonah 4:2 (the eventual stated motive, outside this passage).
- Q8: N/A — Jonah is individuated.
- Q9: Sufficient for the act; insufficient for the motive — named, not filled from outside knowledge.
- Q11: fled (rose-to-flee); fled/paid-and-boarded (continued).

**Decision.** Retain both operations as stated IB acts. The motive driving the flight is recorded as an explicit, named silence, with a flagged forward-pointer to Jonah 4:2 (outside this passage).

### Jon 1:4

> But the Lord hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up.

**Observation.** "The LORD [H3068G] hurled [H2904] a great [H1419A] wind [H7307H] upon [H0413] the sea [H3220G], and there was a mighty [H1419A] tempest [H5591A/H1961] on the sea, so that the ship [H0591] threatened [H2803I] to break [H7665] up."

**Operation 1 — the LORD's act of hurling the wind.**
- **Action-type:** hurled (cast a storm).
- **Subject:** the LORD.
- **Operation:** a movement — an act directed at the sea, and via it the ship.
- **Source:** self — the LORD's own initiative.
- **Target:** the sea (explicit); the ship, and via it its human occupants (in scope per note (b)/(d) — not yet named in this verse).

**Operation 2 — the tempest's effect on the ship.**
- **Action-type:** threatened/imperiled.
- **Subject:** the ship (object, in scope per note (b)/(d) — its peril directly bears on the humans it carries, named as afraid in the next verse).
- **Operation:** a state/status nearing crisis.
- **Source:** the storm — a direct, stated causal chain (Operation 1).
- **Target:** the ship's human occupants (implied; not yet named — that is 1:5).

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: No human is named in this verse. Per step 2 note (d), a verse with only non-human content unrelated to a human would be out of scope — but this content is immediately and explicitly related to the humans named in the surrounding verses (note (d)'s own qualifier, and note (b)); retained on that basis.
- Q3: The LORD's act and the ship's peril are both stated. No human interior appears in this verse.
- Q4: Source of the storm = the LORD, explicit ("the LORD hurled"). Source of the ship's peril = the storm, stated directly.
- Q5: Target = the sea (explicit); the ship (explicit); ultimately Jonah, by the chapter's own developing logic — but not named as target in this verse, so held as referential (note (e)), not asserted as stated fact at this point.
- Q6: A movement (hurled) and a state/status (mighty tempest; ship near breaking).
- Q7: Direct linkage back to 1:3 (Jonah's flight, just narrated) — the storm's timing immediately after the flight strongly invites a causal reading, but the text does not state the connection until 1:12 (Jonah's own words) and implicitly 1:7 (the lot); flagged as an open interpretive fork (per B.9), not settled here. Forward linkage to 1:5 (the sailors' fear) and 1:11-13 (the ship's escalating peril).
- Q8: N/A this verse.
- Q9: Sufficient for what is stated; the causal link between Jonah's flight and the storm is named as an insufficiency-at-this-point, resolved only later.
- Q11: hurled (cast a storm); threatened/imperiled (the ship's peril).

**Decision.** Retain both operations. The storm-Jonah causal link is flagged as an open interpretive fork (per B.9), carried forward rather than asserted here.

### Jon 1:5

> Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep.

**Observation.** "The mariners [H4419] were afraid [H3372G], and each [H0376I] cried out [H2199] to his god [H0430J]. They hurled [H2904] the cargo [H3627] that was in the ship [H0591] into the sea [H3220G] to lighten [H7043] it for them. Jonah [H3124] had gone down [H3381] into the inner part [H3411] of the ship [H5600], and had lain down [H7901G], and was fast asleep [H7290]."

**Operation 1 — the mariners' fear and religious cry.**
- **Action-type:** feared/cried-out (each to his own god).
- **Subject:** the mariners (H4419, a professional collective).
- **Operation:** a movement — fear as an impact from the storm, issuing in an outward cry.
- **Source:** the storm (the immediate, stated cause — directly following 1:4).
- **Target:** "his god" (each sailor's own deity — non-human beings, individuated per sailor).

**Operation 2 — the mariners' act of jettisoning cargo.**
- **Action-type:** cast-out/jettisoned.
- **Subject:** the mariners (collective, acting together).
- **Operation:** a movement — practical, self-preserving action, explicitly linked to their fear ("to lighten it for them").
- **Source:** self — their own initiative, enabled/motivated by the stated fear (a direct in-verse linkage).
- **Target:** the sea (object); the ship (relieved).

**Operation 3 — Jonah's descent and sleep.**
- **Action-type:** went-down/lay-down/slept.
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a state/status — withdrawal and unconsciousness, narrated in stark contrast to the mariners' fear-driven activity in the same verse.
- **Source:** self — his own act; no external cause stated.
- **Target:** n/a directly; relationally, a contrast-target against the mariners' fear (Q7).

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: The mariners — focused inner beings as a collective (Q8); their fear is explicitly stated, not inferred. Jonah — again only his outward state (asleep) is stated; sleeping through a life-threatening storm invites an obvious question (un-fear? exhaustion? evasion continuing from 1:3?) the text does not resolve — carried forward as an emergent item, not settled by importing a reading.
- Q3: Mariners' fear — stated, doubly marked (fear plus the cry it produces). Jonah's sleep — stated as an outward fact; the disposition behind it is not stated — a candidate silence, and a striking one given the contrast the text visibly stages.
- Q4: Source of mariners' fear = the storm, stated. Source of the jettison = their own initiative, enabled by fear (linkage). Source of Jonah's descent/sleep = self; no external cause given.
- Q5: Target of the mariners' cry = their own gods (individuated, "each... his god"); target of the jettison = the sea/ship. Jonah's state has no stated target.
- Q6: Movement (fear, cry, jettison) alongside state/status (Jonah's sleep).
- Q7: **Strong intra-verse linkage/contrast**: the mariners' escalating fear-driven activity is placed directly against Jonah's descent-and-sleep in the same verse — a deliberate structural juxtaposition (their many god-cries vs. his silence; their frantic action vs. his withdrawal), flagged prominently below. Forward linkage to 1:6 (the captain's rebuke of exactly this sleep).
- Q8: "Each [sailor]... his god" treats the collective as an aggregate of individuals each with his own god — a finer-grained collective than "the mariners" alone, distinct from the shared collective act of the jettison.
- Q9: Sufficient for the mariners; insufficient for Jonah's sleep-disposition — named, not filled.
- Q11: feared/cried-out; jettisoned/lightened; went-down/slept.

**Decision.** Retain all three operations. Jonah's sleep is flagged as an open, unresolved interpretive question (carried forward as emergent), not assigned a reading.

### Jon 1:6

> So the captain came and said to him, “ What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish.”

**Observation.** "The captain [H7227B/H2259] came [H7126G] and said [H0559] to him, 'What do you mean [H4100], you sleeper [H7290]? Arise [H6965B], call out [H7121G] to your god [H0430G]! Perhaps [H0194] the god [H0430G] will give a thought [H6245B] to us, that we may not [H3808] perish [H0006].'"

**Operation 1 — the captain's approach and rebuke.**
- **Action-type:** came/rebuked (roused).
- **Subject:** the captain (an individuated role within the collective, distinct from "the mariners" of 1:5).
- **Operation:** a movement — approaching Jonah and confronting him with a question.
- **Source:** self, motivated by the same fear/crisis driving 1:5 (linkage).
- **Target:** Jonah.

**Operation 2 — the captain's command to Jonah.**
- **Action-type:** commanded (arise, call out).
- **Subject:** the captain.
- **Operation:** a movement — an imperative directed at Jonah, echoing the LORD's own command-verb "arise" from 1:2.
- **Source:** self.
- **Target:** Jonah; via him, "your god."

**Operation 3 — the captain's stated hope.**
- **Action-type:** hoped (perhaps... will give a thought).
- **Subject:** the captain.
- **Operation:** a state — a tentative, hedged hope.
- **Source:** self.
- **Target:** "the god" (from the captain's outside perspective, not yet knowing it is the LORD specifically); on behalf of "us" (the ship's whole company, Q8).

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: The captain — a new individuated human, focused inner being; the implied disposition is alarm and desperate hope, continuing the fear established in 1:5. Jonah — addressed directly by another human command, but his own reception is not stated in this verse either; the narrative moves straight to 1:7 without recording any reply from him to the captain at all.
- Q3: The captain's rebuke and hope are stated. Jonah's reception of the rebuke is unstated — a distinct and notable silence, since Jonah is never shown replying to the captain specifically (his first recorded speech in the book comes only at 1:9, answering a different, later question).
- Q4: Source of the captain's alarm/command = self, continuing from the ship-wide fear of 1:5 (linkage). Source of Jonah's non-response = wholly unstated.
- Q5: Target = Jonah (rebuke, command); "the god"/"us" (the hope).
- Q6: Movement (came, commanded) and state (hoped).
- Q7: **Direct verbal linkage to 1:2**: "Arise" (H6965) is the same command-word the LORD used to send Jonah to Nineveh — now spoken to Jonah by a pagan ship's captain, urging him to do what the LORD's own prophet is not doing — one of the strongest ironic linkages in the passage, flagged prominently below. Also links to 1:5 (the captain's fear-source) and forward to 1:7 (the lots, since Jonah still does not visibly comply here either).
- Q8: "Us" (the captain's hoped-for beneficiaries) = the ship's whole company, a collective; the captain speaks representatively for all aboard.
- Q9: Sufficient for what is stated; Jonah's non-response is named as a silence, not an extract gap.
- Q11: came/rebuked; commanded (arise/call out); hoped.

**Decision.** Retain all three operations. Jonah's total silence in response to the captain is flagged as a distinct, pointed silence, carried forward as part of the emerging pattern (see passage-level linkages).

### Jon 1:7

> And they said to one another, “ Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.

**Observation.** "They said [H0559] to one another [H0376I/H7453], 'Come [H1980K], let us cast [H5307I] lots [H1486], that we may know [H3045] on whose account [H4310] this evil [H7451I] has come upon us [H5307I/H9035].' They cast lots [H1486], and the lot [H1486] fell [H5307I] on Jonah [H3124]."

- **Operation:** a movement — mutual speech, proposing a means of discovering the storm's cause.

- **Target:** one another (mutual); the intended outcome (an unnamed party, to be revealed) is referential.

**Operation 2 — the casting and outcome of the lot.**
- **Action-type:** cast/fell (the lot singled out Jonah).
- **Subject:** the sailors (agents of the casting); the lot's outcome as the operative event.
- **Operation:** a movement — the lot "falling on" Jonah.

- Q3: The proposal and its execution are stated. The lot's outcome ("fell on Jonah") is stated as a bare fact, with no interpretive gloss added at this point.
- Q4: Source of the proposal = the sailors, self. Source of the lot's outcome = the mechanism itself, unglossed — an interpretive fork (does the text intend the lot as divinely directed, per convention, or does it withhold that judgment?), not settled here (per B.9), carried forward.
- Q5: Target = "one another" (proposal); Jonah (lot's outcome).
- Q6: Movement throughout.

- Q11: proposed/deliberated; cast/fell (lot).

### Jon 1:8

> Then they said to him, “ Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?”

**Observation.** "They said [H0559] to him, 'Tell [H5046] us on whose account [H0834A/H4310] this evil [H7451I] has come upon us. What is your occupation [H4399]? Where [H0370] do you come [H0935G] from? What is your country [H0776G]? Of what people [H5971A] are you [H0859A]?'"

**Operation 1 — the sailors' interrogation of Jonah.**
- **Action-type:** interrogated/questioned.
- **Subject:** the sailors (collective, now addressing Jonah directly, having identified him by lot).
- **Operation:** a movement — a rapid-fire series of five questions.
- **Source:** self, continuing the fear-driven investigation (linkage to 1:7).
- **Target:** Jonah.

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: The sailors — continuing collective focused inner being, driven by the same fear/need-to-know established since 1:5. Jonah — the addressee; the questions invite, but do not themselves state, his interior.
- Q3: The five questions are stated in full. Jonah's interior at being so interrogated is not stated in this verse — silence, resolved at 1:9's reply (though the reply addresses only some of the questions, see Q9).
- Q4: Source of the interrogation = the sailors, self, continuing their fear (linkage to 1:5-7).
- Q5: Target = Jonah, exclusively and intensively.
- Q6: Movement — a barrage of questioning.
- Q7: Direct linkage to 1:7 (the lot that provoked this) and forward to 1:9 (Jonah's answer) — note the answer addresses only the "who are you/what god" dimension, while the sailors' first and most urgent question ("on whose account") is not restated as directly answered until 1:10's reaction connects the pieces; flagged, not asserted beyond what the text shows.
- Q8: The sailors act as one interrogating body here (contrast 1:5's individuated god-cries).
- Q9: Sufficient for the questions asked; insufficient to know from this verse alone which question Jonah's answer primarily addresses — resolved partially at 1:9-10.

**Decision.** Retain. Jonah's silence at being questioned is carried forward, not resolved until 1:9 — and even then, only his words are given, not a separate statement of his interior state.

### Jon 1:9

> And he said to them, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

**Observation.** "He said [H0559] to them, 'I [H0589] am a Hebrew [H5680], and I fear [H3373] the LORD [H3068G], the God [H0430G] of heaven [H8064], who [H0834A] made [H6213H] the sea [H3220G] and the dry [H3004] land.'"

- **Target:** the sailors (the answer's addressees); the LORD (the object of the stated fear, named explicitly as "the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land").

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — focused inner being; here, for the only time so far, his own interior (fear/reverence toward the LORD) is directly stated in his own voice, not inferred from an act.
- Q3: Stated, explicitly, first person — not inferred.
- Q4: Source of Jonah's stated fear = self. The object of that fear = the LORD, explicitly named with a description ("made... the sea") that directly names the very domain currently in violent motion against the ship — a juxtaposition the text does not spell out further but that sits inside the same verse (Q7).
- Q5: Target = the sailors (recipients of the declaration); the LORD (object of the stated fear).
- Q6: A state — Jonah's own stated disposition (though the act of declaring it is itself a movement of speech).
- Q7: **Strong internal irony**: Jonah confesses fear of the very God whose word he has just spent the whole passage fleeing (1:3), and whose command a pagan captain has already urged him, unknowing, to obey (1:6, the "Arise" echo). The confession's content — "made the sea" — directly names the element now imperiling the ship. Flagged prominently below. Also effectively answers (though not by explicit textual statement) the identity-questions of 1:8.
- Q8: N/A — Jonah speaks as an individual.
- Q9: Sufficient.
- Q11: confessed/declared (identity and fear).

**Decision.** Retain — the passage's first and clearest instance of Jonah's own stated interior, flagged as a major turning point and cross-referenced in the passage-level linkages.

### Jon 1:10

> Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, “ What is this that you have done!” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

**Observation.** "The men [H0582] were exceedingly [H1419A/H3374] afraid [H3372G] and said [H0559] to him, 'What is this that you have done [H6213A]!' The men knew [H3045] that he [H1931] was fleeing [H1272] from the presence [H6440H] of the LORD [H3068G], because [H3588A] he had told [H5046] them [H9038]."

**Operation 1 — the sailors' escalated fear.**
- **Action-type:** feared (exceedingly, intensified from 1:5).
- **Subject:** the men (the sailors, collective).
- **Operation:** a movement/state — an intensified impact, explicitly marked as greater than the storm-fear of 1:5.
- **Source:** Jonah's just-given disclosure (1:9's confession plus, per this verse's own explanatory clause, a further disclosure not directly quoted — "he had told them" he was fleeing from the LORD).
- **Target:** their own interior (fear); secondarily Jonah (the confrontational question).

**Operation 2 — the sailors' rebuking question.**
- **Action-type:** rebuked/exclaimed ("what have you done").
- **Subject:** the men.
- **Operation:** a movement — a shocked, accusatory exclamation.
- **Source:** self, explicitly sourced to their newly-intensified fear and the fact just revealed ("for... because").
- **Target:** Jonah.

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: The sailors — continuing collective focused inner being; here the text is unusually explicit about causation — their fear is stated to be sourced in what Jonah told them (a clean, textually stated instance of Q4, rare in this passage). Jonah — the object of both fear and question; the text records his disclosure as a past act, but not his own feeling in disclosing it, nor any reply to this new accusation — the narrative moves to the next collective operation (1:11) without a recorded reply, a further instance of the "spoken of and spoken to, replies selectively recorded" pattern (compare 1:6).
- Q3: The sailors' fear and its cause are both explicitly stated. Jonah's own feeling and his response to this accusation are unstated.
- Q4: Source of the sailors' fear = Jonah's disclosure, explicitly stated — a rare, fully-stated source-chain (though the disclosure's own motive, why Jonah told them at all, remains unstated).
- Q5: Target = Jonah (the rebuke).
- Q6: Movement (fear intensifying, the exclamation) — a state (fear) driving a movement (speech).
- Q7: Direct linkage back to 1:3 (the flight, now explicitly confirmed as known to the sailors) and 1:9 (the confession, now revealed to have included more than directly quoted) — this verse functions as a narrative retrospective. Forward linkage to 1:11.
- Q8: "The men" — continuing collective.
- Q9: Sufficient for what is stated; the exact content of what Jonah "told them" beyond 1:9's quoted words is not given verbatim — a genuine gap in the text's own reporting, not filled from outside assumption.
- Q11: feared (intensified); rebuked/exclaimed.

**Decision.** Retain both operations. Jonah's non-reply to this direct accusation is flagged, continuing the pattern noted at 1:6 and 1:8.

### Jon 1:11

- **Operation:** a state/status — an intensifying condition ("grew more and more tempestuous," a progressive construction).

### Jon 1:12

> He said to them, “ Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you.”

**Observation.** "He said [H0559] to them, 'Pick me up [H5375G] and hurl [H2904] me into the sea [H3220G]; then the sea will quiet down [H8367] for you, for I know [H3045] it is because of me [H0589] that this great [H1419A] tempest [H5591A] has come upon you.'"

**Operation 1 — Jonah's instruction to be thrown overboard.**
- **Action-type:** instructed/offered (self-surrender).
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a movement — a directive concerning his own body, offered to the sailors.
- **Source:** self — his own proposal, in his own voice.
- **Target:** the sailors (recipients); himself (the object of the proposed act).

**Operation 2 — Jonah's stated knowledge/confession of cause.**
- **Action-type:** confessed/acknowledged (culpability).
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a state — a directly stated interior content: "I know it is because of me" — the clearest, most explicit self-attribution in the whole passage.
- **Source:** self — his own first-person acknowledgment.
- **Target:** n/a directly (a self-referential confession), though relationally it answers the sailors' original question from 1:7-8 ("on whose account").

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — focused inner being; here, for the second time (after 1:9), his interior (knowledge/acknowledgment of responsibility) is directly stated, not inferred. The text still does NOT state his feelings about his own impending death (fear, resignation, penitence, relief) — only his stated knowledge and his practical instruction; the emotional register of his self-offering remains unstated, a genuine and notable silence given the gravity of the act (see emergent-questions log).
- Q3: Stated, explicitly, first person — the passage's clearest instance of a stated (not inferred) self-attribution.
- Q4: Source of Jonah's confession = self, stated directly. The storm's ultimate divine sourcing was already given by the narrator (1:4); here Jonah names himself as the storm's occasion ("because of me"), not the LORD as agent — a fine, worth-preserving distinction (Part B.5): he states his own culpability, not a restatement of the LORD's agency.
- Q5: Target = the sailors (instruction); himself (the proposed act's object).
- Q6: Movement (the instruction) and state (the confession).
- Q7: **Major linkage**: this verse directly answers the sailors' original question from 1:8 ("on whose account") — Jonah himself supplies, unprompted, the answer the lot had already pointed to (1:7) and the sailors had already suspected (1:10). It also reverses the direction of every prior Jonah-operation in the passage: until now he has fled (1:3), slept through danger (1:5), been rebuked (1:6), been silent under interrogation (1:6, 1:8, 1:10), and answered only partially (1:9) — here, for the first time, he acts decisively and self-sacrificially. Flagged as the passage's central turning point.
- Q8: N/A — Jonah speaks individually.
- Q9: Sufficient for what is stated; Jonah's emotional/dispositional state in making this offer is a named insufficiency — the text gives his knowledge and his instruction, not his feeling.
- Q11: instructed/offered (self-surrender); confessed/acknowledged (culpability).

**Decision.** Retain both operations — the passage's turning point. Jonah's emotional disposition in making the offer is recorded as an explicit, named silence, not filled.

## Passage-level linkages (Q7)

1. **The "Arise" (H6965) verbal echo.** The LORD's command to Jonah (1:2) and the captain's command to Jonah (1:6) use the same verb — an ironic reversal: a pagan captain unwittingly repeats God's own word to God's own fleeing prophet.
2. **The "presence of the LORD" bracket in 1:3.** Jonah's flight is explicitly framed twice within one verse ("from the presence of the LORD"... "away from the presence of the LORD") as movement away from the LORD.
3. **The storm-agency asymmetry.** The LORD explicitly hurls the storm (1:4), but its cessation (1:15) is not explicitly re-attributed to the LORD within the text — an interpretive fork carried forward (EQ2 below).
4. **The mariners' fear-vocabulary arc.** Undirected/generic fear of the storm plus individuated cries to "his god" (1:5, 1:10) → shared, named address to "the LORD" in crisis (1:14) → settled, reverent, worshipful fear of the LORD, expressed communally in cultic acts (1:16) — the clearest sustained inner-being arc in the whole passage.
5. **Jonah's own stated-interior instances are rare and clustered.** Silence through 1:1, 1:3, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7, 1:8, 1:10 — broken only at 1:9 (confession of fear/identity) and 1:12 (confession of culpability/self-offering) — then silence resumes through 1:15 and 1:17. A deliberate structural rarity: the prophet's own interior is given far less textual space than the pagan sailors' collective interior.
6. **The four-verse compliance sequence.** 1:12 (Jonah's offer) → 1:13 (the sailors' delay/attempted alternative) → 1:14 (their prayer for exemption) → 1:15 (the act performed, vindicated).
7. **The lot's theological status (1:7)** is left unglossed — an open interpretive fork about whether the text intends it as directed or left to chance, not resolved here (EQ3 below).
8. **The LORD's explicit agency bracketing the whole passage**: 1:1-2 (word/command), 1:4 (storm), 1:17 (fish) — with the intervening 1:15 (calming) notably NOT re-stating that agency explicitly.
9. **"Great" (H1419A) recurs** applied to the city (1:2), the wind/tempest (1:4), the fear of the sailors (1:10, 1:16), the tempest again (1:12), and the fish (1:17) — a verbal thread of "greatness" running through divine command, storm, and rescue alike; noted as a recurrence, not asserted as deliberate authorial design beyond the bare fact of it.

## Insufficiencies register

- Jonah's motive for fleeing (1:3) — not stated in this passage; the text's own later explanation (Jonah 4:2) lies outside this passage's scope, named not imported.
- Jonah's disposition while asleep during the storm (1:5) — fear, exhaustion, defiance, spiritual numbness all logically possible, none stated.
- Jonah's reply (if any) to the captain's rebuke (1:6) — none recorded.
- The lot's theological status (1:7) — directed by the LORD, or a neutral mechanism the narrative simply reports — not stated.
- The full content of what Jonah "told" the sailors (1:9-10) beyond the quoted words of 1:9 — the narrator's retrospective reference at 1:10 implies more was said than is directly quoted.
- The sailors' specific motive for rowing back to land rather than immediately complying with Jonah's instruction (1:13) — inferred (reluctance to take a life), not stated.
- The explicit agent of the sea's calming (1:15) — not re-stated as the LORD's act within this verse, unlike 1:4's explicit attribution of the storm's onset.
- Jonah's own experience/interior at the moment of being cast into the sea (1:15) — wholly unstated.
- Jonah's interior throughout his three days/nights in the fish (1:17) — deferred to Jonah 2, outside this passage.

## Emergent questions log (filed against this passage — not merged across passages; resolved, if at all, at the whole-book read)

- **EQ1.** Does Jonah's near-total silence about his own interior (compare the sailors' unusually full arc) reflect a deliberate authorial strategy — the book's irony resting partly on withholding the prophet's own voice while giving the pagans theirs? Carried forward, to be tested against Jonah 2-4, where Jonah does finally speak at length (prayer in ch. 2, direct complaint in ch. 4).
- **EQ2 (interpretive fork, per B.9).** Is the storm's cessation (1:15) implicitly the LORD's own act (continuing 1:4's explicit agency), or does the text's silence there carry independent significance? Carried forward, not settled.
- **EQ3 (interpretive fork).** Is the casting of lots (1:7) presented as divinely directed, per the wider biblical convention (e.g. Prov 16:33), or does this narrative leave it genuinely open, distinct from the explicit divine-agency statements elsewhere in the same chapter (1:1, 1:2, 1:4, 1:17)? Carried forward.
- **EQ4.** The sailors' fear-to-worship arc (1:5→1:10→1:14→1:16) is fully realized within a single chapter for characters never named again in the book. Does this imply the book's inner-being focus, at least in ch. 1, actually falls more heavily on the sailors than on Jonah himself? Carried forward to the whole-book read.
- **EQ5 (action-type recurrence, Q11/B.10 — and the passage's seed instance of the new divine-mirroring question, Q12/B.11, added 2026-07-28).** "Hurled" (H2904) is used three times in this passage: the LORD hurling the wind (1:4), the sailors hurling the cargo (1:5), and the sailors hurling Jonah (1:15) — the same root applied to divine, practical/self-preserving, and human-sacrificial-compliance acts respectively. Read against Q12 (does a human operation compare to, differ from, or invert what the passage shows of God's own action?): the LORD hurls disturbance/judgment at Jonah's own flight (1:4); the sailors hurl cargo out of self-preserving fear (1:5); the sailors hurl Jonah out in reluctant, prayer-covered compliance with Jonah's own self-sacrificial instruction (1:15) — three acts sharing one verb, but the human instances neither simply resemble nor simply oppose the divine one: 1:5 is self-directed survival, unrelated in kind to 1:4's judgment; 1:15 is other-directed and costly, closer in shape to a costly divine act elsewhere in the corpus than to 1:4 itself. The passage's own data does not clearly anchor a specific comparison beyond this bare observation — per B.11, that is recorded as the finding, not elaborated further. Logged for cross-corpus weighing (Q11) and as the seed of the ongoing mirroring question (Q12), not resolved here.
- **EQ6 (action-type recurrence, Q11/B.10).** "Arise" (H6965) recurs at 1:2 (LORD→Jonah) and 1:6 (captain→Jonah) — logged, worth weighing against other prophetic call-narratives in the corpus once more are read. Also a candidate for Q12 (a human, the captain, echoing the LORD's own word without resemblance in authority or content — an ironic non-mirroring more than a mirroring) — carried forward, not asserted.

- Next passage: Jonah 2 (Jonah's prayer from the fish) — the natural continuation point, per 1:17's own forward linkage.
- EQ1-EQ4 (interpretive forks and structural observations) carried forward per B.9/B.8, to be weighed against Jonah 2-4 at the whole-book read, not resolved here.
- The action-type recurrences (EQ5, EQ6) are logged per Q11/B.10 discipline as labels only, not built into a controlled vocabulary at this stage (per B.10's explicit caution against premature formalization).

Future debates apply it where the passage anchors it; this debate is not retrofitted beyond this note.
